title: Sujata's bowl of rice
hookLine: a village woman offers milk-rice; he eats, and the five leave him in disgust
last: JAMBU — THE JOY WAS A CLUE.

lines: A MEAL WHEN YOU NEEDED IT.
cards: Someone has probably made you a meal when you needed it more than you knew. A friend who showed up after a funeral with a casserole. A grandmother who wouldn't let you leave without eating.
A stranger who bought you lunch. Food given at the right moment can feel like being brought back to life. The wanderer has made his decision.
To reach the calm he remembered from the rose-apple tree, he needs a body that can sit. So he's going to eat. Real food.
And in the village of Senani, near Uruvela, lives a young woman named Sujata, who has been preparing a very special bowl of rice.

teach.h: RICE AND BREAD. THE FIVE LEAVE.
teach.b: This meal comes from two places, an old one and a later one. In the Buddha's own account, he simply says: I ate solid food, rice and bread.
And my five companions, who had been waiting for me to find the truth, were disgusted. The wanderer Gotama has become self-indulgent, they said. He's given up the struggle.
And they left him. The later telling gives the meal a face.

teach.h: A VOW AT A BANYAN TREE.
teach.b: Sujata had once made a vow at a banyan tree: if she married well and had a son, she would bring an offering to the spirit of that tree. Her wish came true.
So she prepared the richest milk-rice she could, and sent her servant ahead to clean the place.

The servant saw the thin wanderer sitting under the banyan, glowing in the early light, and ran back: the tree spirit has come in person! Sujata came with a golden bowl of milk-rice and offered it. He accepted, and ate.
Think about who she is. Not a queen, not a priest, not a well-known teacher.

teach.h: A YOUNG MOTHER FEEDS THE WAY.
teach.b: A young mother from a village, keeping a promise. Her bowl gives him the strength for everything that comes next.
That's why Buddhists honor her to this day, and some remember her as one of the Buddha's first supporters. And the five? By the morning of Sujata's bowl they're already gone, sure he's failed.
The people waiting for him to succeed left just before he did.

how: Offering food to monks and nuns is one of the most common Buddhist practices, and many Buddhists remember Sujata's gift; in some places people make milk-rice offerings on Vesak in her memory.

o: the golden bowl that held Sujata's offering
a thin bean soup that ascetics lived on
rice boiled in milk, the dish Sujata offered

games.q: who's at the banyan tree — tap the pairs.
p: offered a golden bowl of milk-rice
thought he was the tree spirit
an offering if she had a son

s: the five companions left because he ate
they thought he'd given up the struggle, just as he was about to succeed.
Sujata is named in the Buddha's own account in MN 36
MN 36 says only that he ate rice and bread. Sujata's name comes from the later telling.
in the telling, Sujata's servant mistook him for the tree spirit
glowing in the early light under the banyan.

games.q: you're one of the five. after six years, the man you've been waiting on starts eating real food. what do you do?
o: eat with him and ask why.
leave in disgust: he's given up.
games.why: they leave, thinking he's become self-indulgent. it's one of the story's ironies: they walked away just as he was about to succeed.

practice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, hold it; if not, picture the last thing you ate, and think of the people behind it: someone who grew it, carried it, cooked it or packed it.
Silently thank them, then take one slow bite or sip, a gift received the way the wanderer received Sujata's bowl. Notice the strength it gives, even a little.

wordCard.voice: Payasa. The milk-rice Sujata offered the starving wanderer, which gave him strength for the night ahead.

orig.note: Pali: milk-rice, rice boiled in milk, the dish Sujata offered.

carryVoice: Your line: feed the one who walks. One bowl, at the right moment, can carry someone a long way. Day forty-eight.
